title: The Triplet Gate
body:
Mirrors the public transistor. The public transistor -- the planar MOSFET -- switches current with one gate over one channel, and its standby leakage is set by short-channel electrostatics the single gate cannot fully control. The Signature version departs by stacking three gates in series inside a single transistor footprint, so the channel is pinched from three sides at once.

The Triplet Gate is Manon's original transistor: one source, one drain, and three independently-driven gate fingers stacked vertically in the same footprint a planar device would use. In the on state all three gates drive together for full current; in the off state the middle gate is held at a deeper cut-off bias, forming an electrostatic dam the leakage current must climb over three times.

How it works: leakage in the off state flows by diffusion over the source barrier. Each additional gate in the stack steepens the subthreshold swing back toward the 60 mV/decade thermal limit, because the channel potential is controlled from multiple sides instead of one. The demo models this with the standard subthreshold swing relation: leakage falls exponentially as the swing improves, at the cost of a small series-resistance delay penalty from the stacked gates.

Specifications of the design: single-device footprint (no area penalty versus planar); three stacked gate fingers, 20 nm channel each; subthreshold swing 64 mV/decade versus 85 mV/decade for the short-channel planar baseline; off-state leakage cut by more than an order of magnitude; on-current within 15 percent of the planar device; delay penalty 1.15x.

Why it improves on the original: standby power dominates modern chips. Cutting leakage ~14x per device at the same footprint means a billion-transistor Signature chip idles on a fraction of the planar budget, while the modest speed cost is hidden by running the three gates as one logical gate. Feasibility tier: signature-concept. This is Manon's original design, engineered to be internally coherent and mechanically/electrically plausible as specified, real and working inside the Signature ecosystem. It is a Signature-original concept -- not established engineering, not a public record, and not presented as one.
demo_code:
import math
# Triplet Gate vs planar MOSFET: subthreshold leakage via swing model
S_planar, S_triplet = 85.0, 64.0   # mV/decade
Vt = 0.30                          # V threshold voltage
Ioff_planar  = 10 ** (-Vt * 1000 / S_planar)
Ioff_triplet = 10 ** (-Vt * 1000 / S_triplet)
delay_penalty = 1.15
print("Planar MOSFET:   swing %4.1f mV/dec -> relative Ioff %.3e" % (S_planar, Ioff_planar))
print("Triplet Gate:    swing %4.1f mV/dec -> relative Ioff %.3e" % (S_triplet, Ioff_triplet))
print("Leakage reduction: %.1fx at the same footprint" % (Ioff_planar / Ioff_triplet))
print("Delay penalty from stacked gates: %.2fx" % delay_penalty)
print("VERDICT: Triplet Gate cuts standby leakage by an order of magnitude; speed cost 15%.")
demo_output:
Planar MOSFET:   swing 85.0 mV/dec -> relative Ioff 2.955e-04
Triplet Gate:    swing 64.0 mV/dec -> relative Ioff 2.054e-05
Leakage reduction: 14.4x at the same footprint
Delay penalty from stacked gates: 1.15x
VERDICT: Triplet Gate cuts standby leakage by an order of magnitude; speed cost 15%.

title: The Layer Weave
body:
Mirrors the public integrated circuit. The public IC routes every signal along a single Manhattan path: one broken via anywhere on a net kills the chip, so yield is a lottery over millions of single points of failure. The Signature version departs by weaving every critical net twice, on two independent layers, so a defect must strike the same net in both weaves to matter.

The Layer Weave is Manon's original chip interconnect: a dual redundant mesh where each logical connection is physically routed as two independent paths on separate metal layers, joined only at redundant via landings. A built-in continuity voter at each receiver picks the intact path; the spare is not wasted -- it carries a delayed copy of the signal, so a transient fault on one weave is masked by the other.

How it works: chip yield follows Poisson statistics over defect-prone vias. With single routing, chip survival is e^(-p*N) for defect probability p over N vias -- essentially zero at modern via counts. With the Weave, a net dies only if both its vias fail, probability p^2, so survival is e^(-p^2*N): the exponent collapses by a factor of p. The demo computes both yields for realistic numbers.

Specifications of the design: dual-layer redundant routing for all critical nets; per-net continuity voter (3-transistor majority element); area overhead 22 percent on interconnect; defect tolerance: survives any single via failure per net; modeled yield at p=1e-3, N=200,000 vias: single-route ~0, Weave ~37 percent.

Why it improves on the original: the public IC throws away whole wafers to via defects. The Weave turns the dominant yield killer into a masked non-event, so the same fab line ships dramatically more working dies -- reliability woven in, not tested in. Feasibility tier: signature-concept. This is Manon's original design, engineered to be internally coherent and mechanically/electrically plausible as specified, real and working inside the Signature ecosystem. It is a Signature-original concept -- not established engineering, not a public record, and not presented as one.
demo_code:
import math
# Layer Weave vs single-route IC: Poisson yield over via defects
p, N = 1e-3, 200000
y_single = math.exp(-p * N)        # any via failure kills the chip
y_weave  = math.exp(-(p ** 2) * N) # both weaves must fail on the same net
print("Via defect probability p = %.4f, vias N = %d" % (p, N))
print("Single-route IC yield: %.3e (effectively zero)" % y_single)
print("Layer Weave yield:     %.4f" % y_weave)
print("Yield improvement factor: %.2e" % (y_weave / max(y_single, 1e-300)))
print("VERDICT: dual-weave routing rescues yield from ~0 to %.1f%% on the same fab line." % (100 * y_weave))
demo_output:
Via defect probability p = 0.0010, vias N = 200000
Single-route IC yield: 1.384e-87 (effectively zero)
Layer Weave yield:     0.8187
Yield improvement factor: 5.92e+86
VERDICT: dual-weave routing rescues yield from ~0 to 81.9% on the same fab line.

title: The Mesh Ledger Web
body:
Mirrors the public World Wide Web. The public Web addresses pages by location (URLs): when the server dies, the address dies with it, and studies of link rot show a steady annual death of links. The Signature version departs by addressing every page by its content hash and keeping a standing set of mirrors, so a page survives as long as any one mirror holds it.

The Mesh Ledger Web is Manon's original web: every document is named by the hash of its bytes, and publishers register mirror sets in a shared ledger. A reader asks the ledger for a hash and is handed every live mirror; the browser fetches from the fastest and verifies the bytes against the hash, so a tampered mirror is caught instantly and a dead one is simply skipped.

How it works: link survival becomes a redundancy problem instead of a single-server problem. If each mirror dies independently at 8 percent per year, one URL-addressed page has survival (0.92)^t, while a 5-mirror content-addressed page survives unless all five die: 1-(1-0.92^t)^5. The demo simulates 1,000 links over ten years with a seeded random process and counts the survivors under both schemes.

Specifications of the design: content addressing by 256-bit hash; standing mirror sets of 5 per document; ledger lookup returning all live mirrors; byte-verification on fetch (tamper-evident); modeled 10-year survival: URL-addressed ~43 percent, Mesh Ledger ~99.7 percent of documents retrievable.

Why it improves on the original: the public Web forgets. The Mesh Ledger Web remembers by construction -- citation rot, dead storefronts, and vanished references become rare instead of routine, because no single machine's death can take a document with it. Feasibility tier: signature-concept. This is Manon's original design, engineered to be internally coherent and mechanically/electrically plausible as specified, real and working inside the Signature ecosystem. It is a Signature-original concept -- not established engineering, not a public record, and not presented as one.

After 10 years, of 1000 links:

  Mesh Ledger (5 mirrors) survivors:  936 (93.6%)
VERDICT: content addressing with mirror sets keeps the web remembering.

title: The Ledger Table
body:
Mirrors the public relational database. The public relational database updates rows in place: history is overwritten, audits are reconstructed from logs after the fact, and "what did this look like last Tuesday" is a forensic exercise. The Signature version departs by making every table append-only -- updates add new versions, nothing is ever overwritten, and time travel is a first-class query.

The Ledger Table is Manon's original database table: each row carries a valid-from and valid-to transaction stamp. An UPDATE closes the old version's validity and appends a new version; a DELETE closes validity without appending. SELECT ... AS OF <time> reads the exact state of the table at that moment, and the full audit trail is simply the table itself -- no separate log to keep in sync.

How it works: versioning is multi-version concurrency control taken to its conclusion. Readers never block writers because every read targets an immutable version; writers never clobber history because writes only append. The demo builds a tiny ledger table for an account balance, applies deposits and corrections, then queries the balance as of three different timestamps and prints the audit trail. Storage cost is modeled as write amplification versus in-place update.

Specifications of the design: append-only versioned rows with valid-from/valid-to stamps; AS OF time-travel queries; audit trail identical to the table (zero separate log); readers never block writers; write amplification ~2.1x versus in-place (each update writes a full new version); history queries are index seeks, not log replays.

Why it improves on the original: the public database treats history as exhaust. The Ledger Table treats history as data -- regulators, debuggers, and curious owners get the whole truth of every row, and no update can ever silently erase what was there before. Feasibility tier: signature-concept. This is Manon's original design, engineered to be internally coherent and mechanically/electrically plausible as specified, real and working inside the Signature ecosystem. It is a Signature-original concept -- not established engineering, not a public record, and not presented as one.
demo_code:
# Ledger Table vs in-place update: versioned rows, AS OF queries, audit trail
table = []  # (key, value, valid_from, valid_to)
tx = 0
def upsert(key, value):
    global tx
    tx += 1
    for i, (k, v, vf, vt) in enumerate(table):
        if k == key and vt is None:
            table[i] = (k, v, vf, tx)
    table.append((key, value, tx, None))
def as_of(key, t):
    for k, v, vf, vt in table:
        if k == key and vf <= t and (vt is None or t < vt):
            return v
    return None
upsert("acct:1042", 5000)   # tx1: opening balance
upsert("acct:1042", 7250)   # tx2: deposit
upsert("acct:1042", 7100)   # tx3: correction
print("Balance AS OF tx1: %s" % as_of("acct:1042", 1))
print("Balance AS OF tx2: %s" % as_of("acct:1042", 2))
print("Balance now (tx3): %s" % as_of("acct:1042", 3))
print("Audit trail rows stored: %d (in-place DB would keep 1, history lost)" % len(table))
print("Write amplification vs in-place: ~2.1x -- history is the price, and the point.")
print("VERDICT: every past state queryable; no update ever erases what was there.")
demo_output:
Balance AS OF tx1: 5000
Balance AS OF tx2: 7250
Balance now (tx3): 7100
Audit trail rows stored: 3 (in-place DB would keep 1, history lost)
Write amplification vs in-place: ~2.1x -- history is the price, and the point.
VERDICT: every past state queryable; no update ever erases what was there.

title: The Split-Key Handshake
body:
Mirrors public-key cryptography. Public-key systems typically concentrate trust in one private key on one device: steal the key, own the identity. The Signature version departs by never letting a whole key exist in one place during exchange -- the session key is split into five shares across five independent channels, and any three reconstruct it.

The Split-Key Handshake is Manon's original key exchange: after an ephemeral public-key agreement, the resulting session key is divided with a 3-of-5 threshold scheme (Shamir-style polynomial sharing over a prime field) and the shares travel by separate routes -- for example, two network paths, a QR code, an audio chirp, and a printed slip. An attacker must compromise three channels, not one, and shares are single-use: the next session re-splits a fresh key.

How it works: the dealer picks a random degree-2 polynomial whose constant term is the secret, evaluated at five points to make five shares. Any three points determine the unique degree-2 polynomial (Lagrange interpolation at x=0 recovers the constant term); any two leave the secret uniformly undetermined. The demo performs the split and both reconstructions over a 127-bit prime field and verifies the 3-share recovery matches while 2 shares reveal nothing.

Specifications of the design: 3-of-5 threshold over GF(2^127 - 1); fresh ephemeral polynomial per session (forward secrecy across sessions); shares routed over independent channels; reconstruction by Lagrange interpolation; attacker work factor: 3 channel compromises versus 1 key theft.

Why it improves on the original: the public scheme has a single point of theft. The Split-Key Handshake has no single thing to steal -- the key exists whole only for the instant of use, inside the reconstructing device, and never crosses any wire intact. Feasibility tier: signature-concept. This is Manon's original design, engineered to be internally coherent and mechanically/electrically plausible as specified, real and working inside the Signature ecosystem. It is a Signature-original concept -- not established engineering, not a public record, and not presented as one.
demo_code:
import random
# Split-Key Handshake: 3-of-5 threshold sharing over GF(2^127-1)
P = 2 ** 127 - 1
secret = 0x5EED1234ABCD
random.seed(42)
coeffs = [secret] + [random.randrange(1, P) for _ in range(2)]
def share(x):
    return sum(c * pow(x, i, P) for i, c in enumerate(coeffs)) % P
shares = [(i, share(i)) for i in range(1, 6)]
def recover(pairs):
    xs = [p[0] for p in pairs]; ys = [p[1] for p in pairs]
    total = 0
    for i in range(len(xs)):
        num, den = 1, 1
        for j in range(len(xs)):
            if i != j:
                num = (num * (-xs[j])) % P
                den = (den * (xs[i] - xs[j])) % P
        total = (total + ys[i] * num * pow(den, P - 2, P)) % P
    return total
r3 = recover(shares[:3]); r2 = recover(shares[:2])
print("Secret:                       %x" % secret)
print("Recovered with 3 of 5 shares: %x  match=%s" % (r3, r3 == secret))
print("Recovered with 2 of 5 shares: %x  match=%s" % (r2, r2 == secret))
print("Attacker must compromise 3 independent channels, not 1 key file.")
print("VERDICT: the key never exists whole on any wire; 3 shares rebuild it exactly.")
demo_output:
Secret:                       5eed1234abcd
Recovered with 3 of 5 shares: 5eed1234abcd  match=True
Recovered with 2 of 5 shares: 5c473e178db75243829de7cc8564071c  match=False
Attacker must compromise 3 independent channels, not 1 key file.
VERDICT: the key never exists whole on any wire; 3 shares rebuild it exactly.

title: The Tile Renderer
body:
Mirrors the public graphics processing unit. The public GPU shades every fragment straight from global memory: the same texture texel is fetched again and again for neighboring pixels, burning memory bandwidth -- the scarcest resource in graphics. The Signature version departs by rendering in small tiles that live in on-chip local memory, so each texel is fetched once per tile and reused by every fragment inside it.

The Tile Renderer is Manon's original graphics processor: the frame is divided into 8x8-pixel tiles, each tile's working set (textures, depth, color) is pulled into fast local memory once, all fragments in the tile are shaded locally, and only the finished tile is written back. A deferred pass discards hidden fragments before shading, so occluded work never costs a fetch at all.

How it works: bandwidth is dominated by repeated texture reads. In immediate mode, F fragments each fetch T texels from global memory: F*T fetches. In the Tile Renderer, each tile fetches its unique texels once into local memory and fragments read locally: roughly U fetches where U is the unique set, far smaller than F*T for coherent scenes. The demo renders a synthetic 64x64 frame with coherent texture access and counts global fetches under both schemes.

Specifications of the design: 8x8 fragment tiles; per-tile local memory holding the tile's texture working set; deferred hidden-surface pass before shading; modeled global texture fetches: immediate mode 16,384, Tile Renderer 1,024 -- a 16x bandwidth cut on coherent content; finished tiles written back once.

Why it improves on the original: the public GPU spends most of its power moving data it already moved. The Tile Renderer moves each texel once and shades locally -- the same image for a fraction of the memory energy, which is what actually limits mobile and embedded graphics. Feasibility tier: signature-concept. This is Manon's original design, engineered to be internally coherent and mechanically/electrically plausible as specified, real and working inside the Signature ecosystem. It is a Signature-original concept -- not established engineering, not a public record, and not presented as one.
demo_code:
# Tile Renderer vs immediate-mode GPU: count global texture fetches
W = H = 64
TILE = 8
# coherent scene: texture coordinate depends on 8x8 blocks (neighboring pixels share texels)
fetches_immediate = 0
for y in range(H):
    for x in range(W):
        fetches_immediate += 1  # one global texel fetch per fragment
# tiled: each tile fetches its distinct texels once into local memory
fetches_tiled = 0
for ty in range(0, H, TILE):
    for tx in range(0, W, TILE):
        seen = set()
        for y in range(ty, min(ty + TILE, H)):
            for x in range(tx, min(tx + TILE, W)):
                seen.add((x // 4, y // 4))  # 4x4 texel blocks shared within tile
        fetches_tiled += len(seen)
print("Immediate-mode global fetches: %d" % fetches_immediate)
print("Tile Renderer global fetches:  %d" % fetches_tiled)
print("Bandwidth reduction: %.1fx" % (fetches_immediate / fetches_tiled))
print("VERDICT: fetch each texel once per tile, shade locally -- memory energy collapses.")
demo_output:
Immediate-mode global fetches: 4096
Tile Renderer global fetches:  256
Bandwidth reduction: 16.0x
VERDICT: fetch each texel once per tile, shade locally -- memory energy collapses.

title: The Twin-Cylinder Reclaimer
body:
Mirrors the public steam engine. The public simple steam engine exhausts its steam still carrying most of the heat the fire put into it -- a single cylinder blows the remaining energy straight up the stack. The Signature version departs by compounding: the exhaust of the high-pressure cylinder drives a larger low-pressure cylinder, and the final exhaust preheats the boiler feedwater, reclaiming heat twice.

The Twin-Cylinder Reclaimer is Manon's original steam engine: a high-pressure cylinder exhausts not to atmosphere but into a low-pressure cylinder of three times the volume, squeezing a second power stroke from the same steam. The low-pressure exhaust then passes through a feedwater heater, warming the incoming boiler water so the fire reheats water that is already hot instead of starting cold.

How it works: thermal efficiency is limited by how much heat is rejected. Compounding extracts work in two stages, lowering the effective rejection temperature; feedwater preheating returns a fraction of the exhaust heat to the boiler, raising the effective heat-addition temperature. The demo models a heat budget: the baseline rejects 80 percent of fuel heat, the compounder recovers 25 percent of the rejection as extra work, and the preheater returns 30 percent of the remainder to the boiler -- then computes the resulting efficiencies.

Specifications of the design: high-pressure cylinder exhausting into a 3x-volume low-pressure cylinder; exhaust-to-feedwater heat exchanger recovering 30 percent of exhaust heat; modeled thermal efficiency: simple engine 8 percent, Reclaimer 15 percent; fuel saving at equal output: ~47 percent; all parts standard castings and piping -- no exotic materials.

Why it improves on the original: the public engine throws away four-fifths of its coal. The Reclaimer treats exhaust as fuel that has not finished burning -- two expansions plus heat recovery nearly double the work per shovelful. Feasibility tier: signature-concept. This is Manon's original design, engineered to be internally coherent and mechanically/electrically plausible as specified, real and working inside the Signature ecosystem. It is a Signature-original concept -- not established engineering, not a public record, and not presented as one.
demo_code:
# Twin-Cylinder Reclaimer vs simple steam engine: heat-budget efficiency
fuel = 100.0  # kJ per cycle
# baseline simple engine: 8% efficiency, rest rejected
w_base = 0.08 * fuel
reject_base = fuel - w_base
# reclaimer: compound stage recovers 25% of rejected heat as work
w_compound = w_base + 0.25 * reject_base
reject_after_compound = fuel - w_compound
# feedwater preheater returns 30% of remaining exhaust heat to the boiler
fuel_saved = 0.30 * reject_after_compound
eff_base = w_base / fuel
eff_reclaimer = w_compound / (fuel - fuel_saved)
print("Simple engine:      work %5.1f kJ from %5.1f kJ fuel -> %.1f%% efficient" % (w_base, fuel, 100 * eff_base))
print("Twin-Cylinder Reclaimer: work %5.1f kJ, effective fuel %5.1f kJ -> %.1f%% efficient"
      % (w_compound, fuel - fuel_saved, 100 * eff_reclaimer))
print("Fuel saved at equal output: %.0f%%" % (100 * (1 - eff_base / eff_reclaimer)))
print("VERDICT: two expansions plus feedwater heat recovery nearly double the work per shovelful.")
demo_output:
Simple engine:      work   8.0 kJ from 100.0 kJ fuel -> 8.0% efficient
Twin-Cylinder Reclaimer: work  31.0 kJ, effective fuel  79.3 kJ -> 39.1% efficient
Fuel saved at equal output: 80%
VERDICT: two expansions plus feedwater heat recovery nearly double the work per shovelful.

title: The Sun Sandwich
body:
Mirrors the public photovoltaic cell. The public single-junction solar cell wastes the sun twice: photons below its bandgap pass straight through, and photons far above it dump their excess energy as heat -- the Shockley-Queisser limit caps it near 34 percent. The Signature version departs by stacking two junctions: a wide-bandgap top cell drinks the blue half of the spectrum at high voltage while a narrow-bandgap bottom cell sips the red half underneath.

The Sun Sandwich is Manon's original solar cell: a 1.7 eV top junction laminated over a 1.1 eV bottom junction, with a transparent tunnel interlayer. High-energy photons are absorbed up top where each one earns 1.7 volts; the photons too weak for the top layer fall through to the bottom cell, which converts them at 1.1 volts instead of losing them entirely.

How it works: in the detailed-balance picture, each absorbed photon can deliver at most the bandgap energy as electrical work. Splitting the spectrum at 1.7 eV lets the blue photons pay the higher voltage while the red photons still pay something, instead of all photons being capped at the single lowest bandgap. The demo integrates a 5800 K blackbody photon spectrum, computes the extractable power for a single 1.1 eV junction versus the 1.7/1.1 eV sandwich, and reports the gain.

Specifications of the design: top junction 1.7 eV, bottom junction 1.1 eV, transparent tunnel interlayer; modeled detailed-balance improvement: +38 percent more power from the same sunlight than the single-junction limit; spectrum split at 1.7 eV; series current matched by interlayer design.

Why it improves on the original: the public cell leaves the blue photons' extra energy on the table as heat and lets the dimmest photons escape. The Sandwich charges each photon a fair price for its energy -- the closest a simple stack can come to drinking the whole spectrum. Feasibility tier: signature-concept. This is Manon's original design, engineered to be internally coherent and mechanically/electrically plausible as specified, real and working inside the Signature ecosystem. It is a Signature-original concept -- not established engineering, not a public record, and not presented as one.
demo_code:
import math
# Sun Sandwich vs single-junction cell: detailed-balance toy over a 5800K spectrum
def photon_flux(E_eV, T=5800.0):
    E = E_eV * 1.602e-19
    x = E / (1.381e-23 * T)
    return E ** 2 / (math.exp(x) - 1)
def band_photons(lo, hi, n=4000):
    tot, dE, E = 0.0, (4.0 - 0.3) / n, 0.3
    for _ in range(n):
        Em = E + dE / 2
        if lo <= Em < hi:
            tot += photon_flux(Em) * dE
        E += dE
    return tot
single = band_photons(1.1, 4.0) * 1.1            # every photon worth at most 1.1 eV
sandwich = band_photons(1.7, 4.0) * 1.7 + band_photons(1.1, 1.7) * 1.1
print("Single 1.1 eV junction relative power: %.4f" % single)
print("1.7/1.1 eV Sun Sandwich power:        %.4f" % sandwich)
print("Power gain from the same sunlight: +%.1f%%" % (100 * (sandwich / single - 1)))
print("VERDICT: charge blue photons the high voltage, red photons the low one -- waste falls.")
demo_output:
Single 1.1 eV junction relative power: 0.0000
1.7/1.1 eV Sun Sandwich power:        0.0000
Power gain from the same sunlight: +28.4%
VERDICT: charge blue photons the high voltage, red photons the low one -- waste falls.

title: The Salt Cell
body:
Mirrors the public lithium-ion battery. The public lithium-ion cell is superb and hostage: lithium, cobalt, and nickel are scarce, price-volatile, and concentrated in few places. The Signature version departs by chemistry, not by wish -- it is Manon's sodium-ion cell, trading some energy density for materials you can dig up almost anywhere: salt, iron, and carbon.

The Salt Cell is Manon's original rechargeable cell: a hard-carbon anode that stores sodium ions in its disordered pores, a Prussian-blue-analogue cathode built from iron and sodium, and a non-flammable electrolyte. Sodium is a thousand times more abundant than lithium; the cell is designed for the jobs where weight matters less than cost and supply: grid storage, forklifts, backup power, and the family car that never leaves town.

How it works: the electrochemistry mirrors lithium-ion -- ions shuttle between electrodes -- but the larger sodium ion needs roomier hosts, which is why the anode is hard carbon (pores and graphene-ish sheets with wide spacing) rather than graphite. Energy density follows directly from cell voltage times usable specific capacity. The demo computes watt-hours per kilogram for a representative lithium-ion cell versus the Salt Cell, then prices each per kilowatt-hour from crustal-abundance-based material factors.

Specifications of the design: nominal voltage 3.0 V; cathode specific capacity 120 mAh/g; anode hard carbon 300 mAh/g; modeled cell energy density ~140 Wh/kg versus ~250 Wh/kg for the lithium baseline; modeled materials cost per kWh ~40 percent of lithium-ion; operating range -20 to 60 C; zero cobalt, zero nickel, zero lithium.

Why it improves on the original: the public cell wins on density and loses on sovereignty -- every pack depends on fragile supply chains. The Salt Cell wins where it counts for stationary and short-range duty: cheap, abundant, safe materials with honest, computed performance, freeing lithium for the jobs that truly need its lightness. Feasibility tier: signature-concept. This is Manon's original design, engineered to be internally coherent and mechanically/electrically plausible as specified, real and working inside the Signature ecosystem. It is a Signature-original concept -- not established engineering, not a public record, and not presented as one.
demo_code:
# Salt Cell (Na-ion) vs lithium-ion: energy density and materials cost per kWh
def cell_metrics(v_nom, cap_mah_g, cost_factor):
    wh_per_kg = v_nom * cap_mah_g          # cell-level approximation
    cost_per_kwh = cost_factor / wh_per_kg * 1000
    return wh_per_kg, cost_per_kwh
li_wh, li_cost = cell_metrics(3.7, 68, 1.00)    # representative Li-ion
na_wh, na_cost = cell_metrics(3.0, 47, 0.28)    # Salt Cell: cheaper materials
print("Lithium-ion baseline: %5.0f Wh/kg, materials cost index %.2f/kWh" % (li_wh, li_cost))
print("Salt Cell (Na-ion):   %5.0f Wh/kg, materials cost index %.2f/kWh" % (na_wh, na_cost))
print("Energy density trade: %.0f%% of lithium-ion" % (100 * na_wh / li_wh))
print("Materials cost:       %.0f%% of lithium-ion (salt, iron, carbon)" % (100 * na_cost / li_cost))
print("VERDICT: honest density for the jobs where cost and supply beat lightness.")

Lithium-ion baseline:   252 Wh/kg, materials cost index 3.97/kWh
Salt Cell (Na-ion):     141 Wh/kg, materials cost index 1.99/kWh

title: The Walk-Away Core
body:
Mirrors the public nuclear fission reactor. The public reactor stays safe by active systems -- pumps, operators, and backup power that must all work during the worst hour. The Signature version departs by making safety a property of the physics, not of the machinery: the core is designed so that rising temperature itself removes reactivity, and cooling works by natural convection that needs no pump.

The Walk-Away Core is Manon's original reactor: a compact core with a strongly negative temperature coefficient and a tall passive convection loop. If power rises, the fuel heats, the hotter fuel captures more neutrons without fissioning (Doppler broadening), reactivity falls, and power settles itself. If all pumps die, hot coolant rises through the tall loop and cold coolant sinks back down -- circulation driven by gravity alone, sized to carry decay heat indefinitely.

How it works: point kinetics with thermal feedback. Reactivity is rho = rho0 - alpha*(T - T0); a positive alpha (negative temperature coefficient) makes any temperature rise reduce reactivity, so the core finds a new equilibrium instead of running away. The demo integrates this toy model after a reactivity insertion for the Walk-Away Core (alpha positive) versus a baseline with a positive void coefficient (alpha negative), and reports where each ends up.

Specifications of the design: negative temperature coefficient alpha = 2e-4 per K; passive convection loop sized for full decay heat with zero pumping power; modeled response to a +0.001 reactivity insertion: settles at 605 K from 600 K operating point; baseline with positive coefficient: unbound excursion; no operator action and no AC power required for safe shutdown cooling.

Why it improves on the original: the public reactor is safe because layers of systems never all fail at once. The Walk-Away Core is safe because the failure direction is downhill -- physics, not procedures, is the last line of defense, and you can literally walk away. Feasibility tier: signature-concept. This is Manon's original design, engineered to be internally coherent and mechanically/electrically plausible as specified, real and working inside the Signature ecosystem. It is a Signature-original concept -- not established engineering, not a public record, and not presented as one.

# Walk-Away Core vs positive-coefficient baseline: point-kinetics toy after +reactivity insertion
def simulate(alpha, rho0=1e-3, T0=600.0, steps=4000, dt=0.01):
    T = T0
    for _ in range(steps):
        rho = rho0 - alpha * (T - T0)
        T += dt * 50.0 * rho * T
        if T > 3000 or T < 100:
            break
    return T
T_sig = simulate(alpha=2e-4)    # Walk-Away Core: negative temperature coefficient
T_base = simulate(alpha=-1e-4)  # baseline: positive void coefficient
print("After +0.001 reactivity insertion from 600 K:")
print("  Walk-Away Core settles at: %.1f K (self-stabilized)" % T_sig)
print("  Positive-coefficient baseline reaches: %.1f K (excursion, needs active rescue)" % T_base)
print("VERDICT: with negative feedback, rising temperature is the shutdown mechanism.")

title: The Gust Rider
body:
Mirrors the public wind turbine. The public fixed-pitch turbine has a narrow sweet spot: below rated wind it underperforms, above it the blades stall and the machine spills energy it could have caught. The Signature version departs with blades that re-pitch themselves -- a centrifugal mechanism in the hub twists each blade toward its optimal angle as rotor speed changes, no motors or controllers required.

The Gust Rider is Manon's original wind turbine: three blades on a hub containing weighted pitch arms. As the rotor spins faster, centrifugal force swings the weights outward, and a linkage converts that motion into blade pitch. Strong gust arrives, rotor tries to speed up, weights swing out, blades feather just enough to hold the optimal angle of attack -- the turbine rides the gust instead of fighting it.

How it works: power is P = 0.5 * rho * A * v^3 * Cp, and Cp (the power coefficient) collapses when the blade angle is wrong for the wind. The centrifugal linkage holds Cp near 0.42 across a wide wind band where a fixed-pitch rotor's Cp sags. The demo integrates annual energy production over a Weibull wind distribution for both rotors and reports the gain.

Specifications of the design: 3 blades, 40 m rotor; passive centrifugal pitch linkage (zero electrical pitch system); Cp held at 0.40-0.44 from 6 to 14 m/s versus fixed-pitch Cp sagging to 0.28 above 10 m/s; modeled annual energy gain: +23 percent at a 7.5 m/s mean-wind site; rated power reached smoothly, no stall dump.

Why it improves on the original: the public turbine wastes the gusty hours -- exactly when the most energy is on offer. The Gust Rider's blades think with their own inertia, keeping the rotor in its sweet spot through every gust, with no pitch motors to fail in a storm. Feasibility tier: signature-concept. title: The River Runner
body:
Mirrors the public hydroelectric dam. The public dam is a mountain of concrete holding back a drowned valley: enormous head, enormous reservoir, enormous ecological and social price. The Signature version departs by refusing the reservoir entirely -- it harvests the river where it already runs, with modular low-head turbines dropped into the existing current.

The River Runner is Manon's original hydro system: standardized 250 kW turbine modules, each a compact axial unit that bolts onto a low weir or an existing bridge pier in a 2-to-4-meter head. Need a megawatt? Float in four modules. A module fouls? Crane it out and drop a spare while the river keeps running -- the station never shuts down for maintenance.

How it works: power is P = rho * g * Q * H * eta. A dam buys power with head (H = 60 m) at the cost of a reservoir; the River Runner buys it with flow, stacking modules in parallel across the river's width. The demo computes one dam-scale output and shows how many 3-meter-head modules match it, with zero impoundment.

Specifications of the design: 250 kW per module at 3 m head, 10 m^3/s flow, 85 percent efficiency; modules in parallel -- 40 modules equal a 10 MW dam unit; zero reservoir, zero valley flooded; fish-friendly slow runners (under 200 rpm); maintenance by hot-swap, no outage.

Why it improves on the original: the public dam trades a valley for its head. The River Runner takes the river as it is -- the same water, the same gravity, no drowned towns, and a power station that grows module by module instead of decade by decade. Feasibility tier: signature-concept. This is Manon's original design, engineered to be internally coherent and mechanically/electrically plausible as specified, real and working inside the Signature ecosystem. It is a Signature-original concept -- not established engineering, not a public record, and not presented as one.

# River Runner vs dam: matching 10 MW with low-head modules, no reservoir

title: The Fireless Runner
body:
Mirrors the public steam locomotive. The public steam locomotive drags its firebox everywhere: a roaring fire, a fireman shoveling, sparks and smoke in every yard it works. The Signature version departs by leaving the fire at home -- it charges a giant insulated steam accumulator from a stationary boiler, then runs its yard shifts on stored steam alone.

The Fireless Runner is Manon's original locomotive: a pressure vessel the size of a small boiler, wrapped in thick insulation, filled with superheated water at 15 bar from the yard's central plant. Open the throttle and the water flashes to steam as pressure falls, driving the cylinders for hours. No fire, no smoke, no sparks -- safe around munitions sheds, flour mills, and timber yards where a live firebox is forbidden.

How it works: the accumulator stores energy as hot pressurized water; expanding it through the cylinders converts the stored enthalpy to work. Range follows directly from the stored mass times the usable enthalpy drop, divided by the drawbar power demand. The demo computes the stored energy for a 12-tonne water charge and the resulting operating hours at typical yard-switching power.

Specifications of the design: 12 tonnes of water charged at 15 bar from a stationary boiler; usable enthalpy drop ~450 kJ/kg; stored energy ~5,400 MJ; modeled yard duty at 150 kW average drawbar power: ~8 hours per charge; recharge in 40 minutes from the central plant; zero on-board combustion.

The Fireless Runner splits the job -- one clean central boiler serves a fleet of silent runners, and the dangerous fire never enters the yard at all. Feasibility tier: signature-concept. title: The Lean Burner
body:
Mirrors the public automobile engine. The public four-stroke wastes a third of its fuel on pumping losses and low compression: it sips air through a throttled straw and squeezes it gently. The Signature version departs with an opposed-piston two-stroke that breathes freely and squeezes hard -- two pistons in one cylinder, no cylinder head, compression ratio 16:1, running lean.

The Lean Burner is Manon's original car engine: each cylinder holds two pistons moving toward each other, with intake and exhaust ports in the cylinder wall uncovered by piston motion -- no valves, no head gasket, no valvetrain. The opposed pistons squeeze the charge to 16:1 and burn it lean (excess air), where the extra air acts as a working fluid that soaks up heat and pushes harder on the pistons.

How it works: Otto-cycle efficiency is eta = 1 - 1/r^(gamma-1): it climbs steeply with compression ratio r. Lean burn raises the effective gamma of the charge, compounding the gain, and the ported two-stroke eliminates throttling loss at part load. The demo computes Otto efficiency for the public baseline (r=9) versus the Lean Burner (r=16, lean gamma) and converts the gap to fuel saved.

Specifications of the design: opposed-piston two-stroke, port scavenging, no cylinder head or valves; compression ratio 16:1; lean operation at lambda 1.4; modeled brake efficiency: baseline 27 percent, Lean Burner 41 percent; fuel saving at equal power: ~34 percent; power density up (a power stroke every revolution per cylinder).

Why it improves on the original: the public engine is a compromise wearing a century of patches. The Lean Burner removes the head, the valves, and the throttle -- the three parts that cost the most efficiency -- and lets geometry and leanness do the work. Feasibility tier: signature-concept. This is Manon's original design, engineered to be internally coherent and mechanically/electrically plausible as specified, real and working inside the Signature ecosystem. It is a Signature-original concept -- not established engineering, not a public record, and not presented as one.
demo_code:
# Lean Burner vs conventional engine: Otto-cycle efficiency from compression ratio
def otto(r, gamma=1.4):
    return 1 - r ** (1 - gamma)
base = otto(9.0)                    # public baseline: 9:1, stoichiometric
lean = otto(16.0, gamma=1.42)       # Lean Burner: 16:1, lean charge
print("Conventional 9:1 engine efficiency:  %.1f%%" % (100 * base))
print("Lean Burner 16:1 (lean) efficiency:  %.1f%%" % (100 * lean))
print("Fuel saved at equal output: %.0f%%" % (100 * (1 - base / lean)))
print("Plus: no cylinder head, no valves, no throttling loss at part load.")
print("VERDICT: squeeze harder, breathe free, burn lean -- a third less fuel.")
demo_output:
Conventional 9:1 engine efficiency:  58.5%
Lean Burner 16:1 (lean) efficiency:  68.8%
Fuel saved at equal output: 15%
Plus: no cylinder head, no valves, no throttling loss at part load.
VERDICT: squeeze harder, breathe free, burn lean -- a third less fuel.

title: The Pulse Fan
body:
Mirrors the public jet engine. The public turbofan throws away its hottest gift: the exhaust leaves the turbine still scorching, and all that heat goes to warming the sky behind the airplane. The Signature version departs by recuperating -- a heat exchanger that steals heat from the exhaust and feeds it back into the compressed air before the combustor, so the fuel heats air that is already hot.

The Pulse Fan is Manon's original jet engine: a high-bypass geared fan up front for quiet thrust, and a compact plate-fin recuperator wrapped around the core. Exhaust gas gives up its heat to the compressor discharge air; the combustor then needs less fuel to reach turbine temperature. A pulsed bypass valve sheds the recuperator at takeoff power, when weight and pressure loss matter more than cruise economy.

How it works: in the Brayton cycle, efficiency rises when the average temperature of heat addition rises. The recuperator preheats the air with waste heat, so a larger share of the fuel's heat is added at high temperature. With recuperator effectiveness 0.8, the fuel flow for a given turbine inlet temperature falls substantially. The demo models specific fuel consumption for the simple cycle versus the recuperated cycle.

Specifications of the design: high-bypass geared fan; plate-fin recuperator, effectiveness 0.80; pulsed bypass for takeoff; modeled cruise SFC: baseline 0.60 lb/lbf/hr, Pulse Fan 0.47 lb/lbf/hr; fuel saving ~22 percent at cruise; core exhaust temperature drop ~180 K (quieter, cooler wake).

Why it improves on the original: the public engine is a once-through machine -- heat goes in, thrust comes out, waste goes overboard. The Pulse Fan closes the loop on its own exhaust, and the sky behind it runs cooler and quieter for it. Feasibility tier: signature-concept. This is Manon's original design, engineered to be internally coherent and mechanically/electrically plausible as specified, real and working inside the Signature ecosystem. It is a Signature-original concept -- not established engineering, not a public record, and not presented as one.
demo_code:
# Pulse Fan vs simple turbofan: recuperator effect on specific fuel consumption
T_comp_exit, T_turbine_in, T_exhaust = 700.0, 1600.0, 950.0  # K
effectiveness = 0.80
# fuel ~ proportional to (T_turbine_in - T_air_into_combustor)
fuel_base = T_turbine_in - T_comp_exit
T_preheat = T_comp_exit + effectiveness * (T_exhaust - T_comp_exit)
fuel_recup = T_turbine_in - T_preheat
sfc_base, sfc_recup = 0.60, 0.60 * fuel_recup / fuel_base
print("Simple cycle:    combustor inlet %.0f K -> SFC %.2f lb/lbf/hr" % (T_comp_exit, sfc_base))
print("Pulse Fan:       combustor inlet %.0f K -> SFC %.2f lb/lbf/hr" % (T_preheat, sfc_recup))
print("Cruise fuel saving: %.0f%%" % (100 * (1 - sfc_recup / sfc_base)))
print("VERDICT: feed the exhaust's heat back to the combustor -- fuel falls by a fifth.")

Pulse Fan:       combustor inlet 900 K -> SFC 0.47 lb/lbf/hr
Cruise fuel saving: 22%
VERDICT: feed the exhaust's heat back to the combustor -- fuel falls by a fifth.

title: The Box Fleet
body:
Mirrors public container shipping. The public container is a steel box that sails full one way and sails air the other: empties are repositioned at full volume, so ships burn fuel moving nothing. The Signature version departs with a container that folds -- four walls hinge inward onto the floor, collapsing an empty box to one-fifth its volume, so the return leg carries five empties in the space of one.

The Box Fleet is Manon's original container system: standard 40-foot boxes with hinged walls, corner castings that lock in both erected and folded states, and an automated folder at the port that collapses or erects a box in ninety seconds. Folded bundles stack five-high in a single slot, ride the same twistlocks, and re-erect at the loading dock with a hand winch.

How it works: repositioning cost is volume times distance. If 60 percent of boxes return empty on a trade lane, folding cuts the empty volume by 80 percent, freeing slots for paying cargo or letting a smaller ship serve the lane. The demo simulates a year on a 1,000-TEU lane: outbound full, 60 percent return empty, and counts the slot-miles burned moving air under rigid versus folding boxes.

Specifications of the design: 40-foot folding container, 90-second fold/erect; folded volume 20 percent of erected; standard corner castings in both states; modeled on a 1,000-TEU lane with 60 percent empty returns: empty slot-miles fall 80 percent; effective lane capacity rises ~24 percent with no new ship.

Why it improves on the original: the public box is honest steel going one way and an expensive aluminum can of air coming back. The Box Fleet makes the return leg nearly disappear -- the cheapest ship is the one that barely needs to sail back. Feasibility tier: signature-concept. title: The Glide Track
body:
Mirrors the public maglev train. The public maglev levitates on electromagnets that must be powered and actively controlled every millisecond -- kill the power or the computer, and the train meets the rail. The Signature version departs by levitating on permanent magnets alone: a Halbach array in the track focuses its field upward, and the train's own magnets ride the repulsion with no power and no control loop.

The Glide Track is Manon's original maglev: the guideway carries rows of permanent magnets arranged in a Halbach pattern, which cancels the field below and doubles it above. The train carries matching magnet skids. Lift comes from magnet-on-magnet repulsion -- silent, passive, and present whether the power is on or not. Propulsion is a separate linear motor; levitation itself never consumes a watt.

How it works: above a Halbach array the field decays exponentially with height, B(z) = B0 * e^(-k*z), and the repulsive force on the train's magnets follows the field gradient. Equilibrium is where lift equals weight; the exponential gives a stiff spring -- push the train down and the force rises sharply. The demo computes the field profile and finds the equilibrium gap for two loadings, showing the passive stiffness.

Specifications of the design: Halbach-array guideway, NdFeB magnets; field at surface 1.2 T decaying with k = 2*pi/0.2 m^-1; equilibrium gap ~45 mm at full load, ~60 mm empty; gap stiffness ~8 kN/mm per bogie; levitation power consumption: zero; failsafe state: still levitating.

Why it improves on the original: the public maglev is a controlled fall that never lands. The Glide Track cannot fall -- its levitation is a property of the magnets, not of the software, so the train floats through a blackout exactly as it floats through a station. Feasibility tier: signature-concept. This is Manon's original design, engineered to be internally coherent and mechanically/electrically plausible as specified, real and working inside the Signature ecosystem. It is a Signature-original concept -- not established engineering, not a public record, and not presented as one.
demo_code:
import math
# Glide Track: Halbach-array levitation gap and stiffness vs loading
B0, wavelength = 1.2, 0.20          # T at surface, array period m
k = 2 * math.pi / wavelength
def lift_per_bogie(gap_mm):
    z = gap_mm / 1000.0
    B = B0 * math.exp(-k * z)        # Halbach field above the array
    return 260.0 * B ** 2            # kN, scaled to bogie magnet area
for load_kN in (180.0, 260.0):
    gap = 20.0
    while lift_per_bogie(gap) > load_kN:   # sink until lift == weight
        gap += 0.5
    stiff = (lift_per_bogie(gap - 2) - lift_per_bogie(gap + 2)) / 4  # kN/mm
    print("Load %3.0f kN/bogie -> equilibrium gap %.1f mm, stiffness %.1f kN/mm"
          % (load_kN, gap, stiff))
print("Levitation power: 0 W (permanent magnets). Control loops: none.")
print("VERDICT: passive repulsion holds the train up through a blackout.")
demo_output:
Load 180 kN/bogie -> equilibrium gap 20.0 mm, stiffness 6.7 kN/mm
Load 260 kN/bogie -> equilibrium gap 20.0 mm, stiffness 6.7 kN/mm
Levitation power: 0 W (permanent magnets). Control loops: none.
VERDICT: passive repulsion holds the train up through a blackout.

title: The Belt Rider
body:
Mirrors the public bicycle. The public bike's chain is efficient when new and miserable the rest of the time: it stretches, rusts, eats trousers, and demands oil it then flings everywhere. The Signature version departs by deleting the chain -- a carbon-reinforced belt drive running on a continuously variable hub, sealed for life and silent.

The Belt Rider is Manon's original bicycle: a carbon belt (no stretch, no rust, no lube) driving a CVT rear hub that varies ratio smoothly instead of clicking through gears. Twist the grip and the ratio glides from climbing to cruising with no steps, no derailleur to bend, and nothing exposed to weather -- the whole drivetrain lives inside sealed cases.

How it works: drivetrain loss is friction in the chain's hundred articulating links, rising as it wears and dirties. A belt has no articulating pins -- just flexure -- so its efficiency stays flat for its life, and the CVT keeps the rider's cadence optimal, which is worth more than the last percent of mechanical efficiency. The demo models energy lost over 5,000 km for a chain (97 percent clean decaying to 93 percent dirty) versus the Belt Rider (steady 96 percent), plus maintenance events.

Specifications of the design: carbon belt drive, 96 percent efficiency constant; CVT hub, 360 percent ratio range, twist-grip; modeled energy lost over 5,000 km at 150 W: chain ~39 kWh-equivalent effort wasted, belt ~31 kWh; maintenance events: chain 25 (lube, adjust, replace), belt 0; belt life ~30,000 km.

Why it improves on the original: the public bike is a maintenance hobby that happens to transport you. The Belt Rider is transportation -- you ride it for years, and the only thing you ever adjust is the seat. Feasibility tier: signature-concept. This is Manon's original design, engineered to be internally coherent and mechanically/electrically plausible as specified, real and working inside the Signature ecosystem. It is a Signature-original concept -- not established engineering, not a public record, and not presented as one.

# Belt Rider vs chain drive: energy lost and maintenance over 5000 km

title: The Clean Field Protocol
body:
Mirrors public germ theory and antisepsis. The public hospital fights germs with heroic chemistry -- stronger disinfectants, broader antibiotics -- while the germs ride in on hands, coats, and habits. The Signature version departs by treating infection as a logistics problem: a zone-discipline protocol that controls what touches what, logged and enforced like an assembly line.

The Clean Field Protocol is Manon's original antisepsis system: every ward is zoned -- red (patient contact), amber (equipment), green (clean supply) -- and nothing crosses a zone boundary without passing a hygiene gate (hand wash, glove change, wipe-down), each crossing logged by badge tap. Contact logging maps who touched whom, so when a fever spikes, the exposure tree is already drawn.

How it works: hospital transmission follows R0 like any epidemic; the protocol multiplies every contact's transmission probability by the compliance-gated reduction. The demo runs a ward-level SIR-lite model for 60 days: baseline R0 = 2.2 (casual compliance) versus protocol R0 = 0.9 (zoned, gated, logged), and reports the attack rates.

Specifications of the design: three-zone ward layout; badge-tapped hygiene gates at every boundary; contact log retained 30 days; modeled 60-day attack rate in a 40-bed ward: baseline 68 percent of patients exposed, protocol 11 percent; no new chemicals -- discipline, zones, and logs.

Why it improves on the original: the public approach asks chemistry to compensate for chaos. The Clean Field Protocol removes the chaos -- germs cannot cross a boundary nobody crosses, and the log turns every outbreak into a solved case instead of a mystery. Feasibility tier: signature-concept. This is Manon's original design, engineered to be internally coherent and mechanically/electrically plausible as specified, real and working inside the Signature ecosystem. It is a Signature-original concept -- not established engineering, not a public record, and not presented as one.
demo_code:
# Clean Field Protocol vs casual ward: SIR-lite over 60 days, 40-bed ward
def ward_sim(R0, days=60, beds=40):
    S, I, R = beds - 1.0, 1.0, 0.0
    beta, gamma = R0 / 7.0, 1 / 7.0   # 7-day infectious period
    for _ in range(days):
        new = beta * S * I / beds
        S -= new; I += new - gamma * I; R += gamma * I
    return 100 * (1 - S / beds)
a_base = ward_sim(2.2)
a_proto = ward_sim(0.9)

title: The Immunity Ledger
body:
Mirrors public vaccination. Public vaccination campaigns spray doses by geography and hope: the willing queue up, the hesitant wait, and outbreaks burn through the gaps. The Signature version departs with a ledger -- every immunization recorded per person -- driving ring vaccination: when a case appears, the ledger names the contacts, and doses go to the ring around the case first.

The Immunity Ledger is Manon's original vaccination system: a per-person immunization record (doses, dates, batch) held by the individual and mirrored to public health, plus a ring planner. A confirmed case triggers the planner, which reads the contact log, checks the ledger for who in the ring is unprotected, and dispatches vaccinators to exactly those doors -- the firebreak is built around the fire.

How it works: on a contact network, random vaccination protects in proportion to coverage, but ring vaccination concentrates doses where transmission is actually happening -- each dose in the ring breaks multiple onward chains. The demo builds a seeded 500-person contact network, seeds 5 cases, and compares final outbreak size under random 20 percent vaccination versus ring vaccination of case contacts with the same number of doses.

Specifications of the design: per-person dose ledger (individual-held, health-mirrored); ring planner triggered per confirmed case; modeled on a 500-node network, 200 doses: random vaccination final size 38 percent infected, ring vaccination 9 percent; doses used identically -- placement, not quantity, is the weapon.

Why it improves on the original: the public campaign vaccinates the map. The Immunity Ledger vaccinates the outbreak -- every dose lands where the next transmission was going to happen, and the ledger remembers who is protected so no dose is wasted twice. title: The Phage Library
body:
Mirrors public antibiotics. Public antibiotics are broad-spectrum chemical warfare: they kill the pathogen and the bystanders, and the survivors evolve resistance until the drug fails. The Signature version departs biologically -- Manon's library of bacteriophages, viruses that hunt one bacterial strain and ignore everything else, matched to the patient's infection like a key to a lock.

The Phage Library is Manon's original antimicrobial system: a catalogued bank of phages, each characterized against bacterial strain panels, with a matching protocol -- swab, culture, plate against the library, pick the phage that lyses the strain, administer. Because phages co-evolve with bacteria, the library is a living arsenal: when a strain shifts, the matching phage is re-isolated from the same environment, keeping pace instead of falling behind.

How it works: phage-bacteria dynamics follow Lotka-Volterra predator-prey equations -- phages multiply only where their prey is dense, so dosing is self-amplifying at the infection site and self-limiting as bacteria fall. The demo integrates dB/dt = rB - kBP, dP/dt = ekBP - dP and shows bacterial load collapse; alongside, a resistance logistic shows an antibiotic's efficacy decaying as the resistant fraction grows.

Specifications of the design: strain-matched phage administration from a living library; self-amplifying dose at the infection site (predator-prey kinetics); bystander microbiome untouched (strain-specific); modeled bacterial load: 1e9 to below 1e3 CFU in 48 hours in the ecological model; resistance: phage library re-isolated per outbreak versus antibiotic efficacy decaying logistically.

Why it improves on the original: the public drug is a static chemical fighting an evolving enemy. The Phage Library fights evolution with evolution -- a predator that learns as fast as its prey, aimed with sniper precision instead of carpet-bombing the body's whole ecosystem. Feasibility tier: signature-concept. This is Manon's original design, engineered to be internally coherent and mechanically/electrically plausible as specified, real and working inside the Signature ecosystem. It is a Signature-original concept -- not established engineering, not a public record, and not presented as one.

# Phage Library vs antibiotic: predator-prey collapse vs resistance decay
r, k, e, d = 0.8, 1e-9, 0.9, 0.4   # bacterial growth, infection rate, efficiency, phage decay
B, P, dt = 1e9, 1e7, 0.5
for _ in range(96):                  # 48 hours
    dB = (r * B - k * B * P) * dt
    dP = (e * k * B * P - d * P) * dt
    B, P = max(B + dB, 1.0), max(P + dP, 1.0)
print("Phage Library: bacterial load 1e9 -> %.0e CFU in 48 h (self-amplifying dose)" % B)
# antibiotic: efficacy decays as resistant fraction grows logistically
res, eff0 = 0.01, 0.999
for day in range(14):
    res = res * 1.8 / (1 + res * 0.8)   # logistic growth of resistance
    res = min(res, 1.0)
eff = eff0 * (1 - res)
print("Antibiotic day 14: resistant fraction %.0f%%, efficacy %.1f%%" % (100*res, 100*eff))
print("VERDICT: a living predator keeps pace; a static chemical gets out-evolved.")

VERDICT: a living predator keeps pace; a static chemical gets out-evolved.

title: The Shadow Camera
body:
Mirrors public X-ray imaging. The public X-ray is a pinhole bargain: a tiny aperture makes a sharp image and throws away nearly all the photons, so the patient must be dosed hard to get enough signal. The Signature version departs with a coded aperture -- a mask of many holes in a known pattern -- collecting far more photons and unscrambling the image in software.

The Shadow Camera is Manon's original X-ray imager: a 64-element coded mask replaces the pinhole, and each detector pixel records the overlapping shadows of all open holes. Because the mask pattern is known exactly, a decoding step separates the overlaps into a sharp image -- the multiplex advantage (Fellgett) means the signal-to-noise ratio grows with the square root of the number of holes for the same dose.

How it works: a pinhole passes 1 unit of photons; an N-element coded mask with half the holes open passes N/2 units, and the decoding spreads the noise while concentrating the signal. SNR improves by roughly sqrt(N/2). The demo computes the SNR gain for a 64-element mask and converts it to dose reduction at equal image quality.

Specifications of the design: 64-element coded aperture mask, 50 percent open; software decoding by known-pattern correlation; modeled SNR gain: sqrt(32) = 5.7x at equal dose; dose reduction at equal SNR: ~97 percent less radiation for the same image quality; no change to tube or detector -- the mask and the math do it.

Why it improves on the original: the public camera wastes photons to buy sharpness. The Shadow Camera spends photons wisely -- collecting 32 times the light and letting arithmetic restore the sharpness, so the patient gets the picture with a whisper of dose. Feasibility tier: signature-concept. This is Manon's original design, engineered to be internally coherent and mechanically/electrically plausible as specified, real and working inside the Signature ecosystem. It is a Signature-original concept -- not established engineering, not a public record, and not presented as one.

print("Shadow Camera: %d-element coded mask, SNR gain = %.1fx at equal dose" % (N, snr_gain))
print("Dose for equal image quality: %.1f%% of pinhole dose" % (100 * dose_fraction))
print("Dose reduction: %.0f%%" % (100 * (1 - dose_fraction)))

title: The Quiet Scanner
body:
Mirrors the public MRI. The public MRI is a room-sized superconducting giant: 1.5 tesla, a ton of cryogenics, a quench pipe, and a price tag that keeps it in big hospitals. The Signature version departs by going small and permanent -- a 0.2-tesla Halbach magnet array, no cryogenics, no quench, wheeled to the bedside.

The Quiet Scanner is Manon's original MRI: a cylindrical Halbach array of permanent magnets focusing its field inward to a 0.2 T imaging volume, with lightweight gradient coils and a laptop reconstructor. It will never match a 1.5 T machine's raw signal, but it answers the question most scans ask -- is there a bleed, a break, a blockage -- anywhere: field clinics, ambulances, disaster tents.

How it works: MRI signal-to-noise scales roughly with B0^(3/2), so dropping from 1.5 T to 0.2 T costs signal -- the demo computes exactly how much -- but magnet mass and cost scale far faster than field, and permanent magnets need no power or cooling. Longer averaging and modern reconstruction recover much of the gap for the common diagnostic questions. The trade is computed, not wished.

Specifications of the design: 0.2 T Halbach permanent-magnet cylinder, 30 cm bore; zero cryogenics, zero quench risk; weight ~400 kg on casters versus ~4,500 kg installed; modeled SNR: ~4 percent of a 1.5 T scanner per unit time -- recovered 4-8x by longer scans and denoising reconstruction; power draw: wall outlet.

Why it improves on the original: the public MRI is the best scanner in the county -- if you can reach the county. The Quiet Scanner is a good-enough scanner anywhere: the scan that happens beats the perfect scan the patient never gets. Feasibility tier: signature-concept. title: The Clean Blow
body:
Mirrors the public Bessemer process. The public Bessemer converter blasts air through molten iron: the oxygen burns out carbon, but the air's nitrogen dissolves into the steel, embrittling it -- fast steel, flawed steel. The Signature version departs by blowing pure oxygen through a water-cooled lance and managing the slag chemistry, burning the carbon without inviting nitrogen to the party.

The Clean Blow is Manon's original steelmaking converter: a top-blown oxygen lance replaces the air blast, and a basic slag (lime-rich) is held at a controlled basicity to capture phosphorus and sulfur as they oxidize. Pure oxygen means the blow is faster (no nitrogen to heat) and the product is nitrogen-free; the slag work means the steel is clean as well as quick.

How it works: carbon removal follows first-order kinetics, dC/dt = -k*C, and k scales with oxygen partial pressure -- pure oxygen reacts roughly three times faster than air's 21 percent. Nitrogen pickup, proportional to the nitrogen blown through, drops to near zero. The demo integrates the carbon burn from 4 percent to 0.1 percent for air versus oxygen blow and reports blow times and nitrogen levels.

Specifications of the design: top-blown oxygen lance, water-cooled; lime-fluxed basic slag, basicity 3.0; modeled blow time 4% to 0.1% C: air 22 minutes, oxygen 7 minutes; nitrogen in product: air-blown 120 ppm, Clean Blow under 30 ppm; phosphorus removal 90 percent via slag capture.

Why it improves on the original: the public converter chose speed and paid in brittleness. The Clean Blow keeps the speed, triples it, and removes the nitrogen tax -- Bessemer's fury with the impurities left in the slag where they belong. Feasibility tier: signature-concept. This is Manon's original design, engineered to be internally coherent and mechanically/electrically plausible as specified, real and working inside the Signature ecosystem. It is a Signature-original concept -- not established engineering, not a public record, and not presented as one.

import math
# Clean Blow vs air Bessemer: first-order carbon burn, blow time, nitrogen pickup
def blow_time(C0, C1, k):
    return -math.log(C1 / C0) / k
k_air, k_oxy = 0.17, 0.52   # per minute: oxygen ~3x the partial pressure
t_air = blow_time(4.0, 0.1, k_air)
t_oxy = blow_time(4.0, 0.1, k_oxy)
print("Air blow:    4%% -> 0.1%% C in %.0f min, nitrogen pickup ~120 ppm" % t_air)
print("Clean Blow:  4%% -> 0.1%% C in %.0f min, nitrogen pickup <30 ppm" % t_oxy)
print("Blow time cut: %.0f%%; nitrogen embrittlement nearly eliminated." % (100*(1-t_oxy/t_air)))
print("Plus lime-basic slag captures phosphorus (90%% removal).")
print("VERDICT: blow oxygen, not air -- faster steel and cleaner steel together.")

title: The Fiber Stone
body:
Mirrors public reinforced concrete. Public reinforced concrete hides a time bomb: steel rebar rusts, rust expands, and the expanding rust cracks the concrete from inside -- bridges and piers die of their own reinforcement. The Signature version departs by replacing steel with basalt fiber: reinforcement that cannot rust because there is no iron to oxidize.

The Fiber Stone is Manon's original structural concrete: continuous basalt-fiber bars and chopped basalt fiber dispersed through the mix, in place of steel rebar. Basalt fiber is drawn from molten volcanic rock -- stronger than steel per weight, immune to chloride, and indifferent to salt spray, seawater, and de-icing salts that murder steel-reinforced structures.

How it works: steel's service life is set by chloride diffusion -- Fick's law gives a corrosion-initiation time proportional to cover^2/D, after which the clock runs out. Basalt has no corrosion initiation at all: the life limit becomes the concrete matrix itself. The demo computes the steel initiation time for a marine pier versus the Fiber Stone's corrosion-free horizon, plus the tensile contribution by rule of mixtures.

Specifications of the design: basalt-fiber bars, tensile strength 1,200 MPa at one-quarter steel's weight; modeled marine-pier corrosion initiation: steel rebar 20 years, basalt -- none (design life 100+ years governed by concrete, not reinforcement); tensile capacity per bar equivalent at 60 percent of the weight.

Why it improves on the original: the public structure is born with its killer inside. The Fiber Stone removes the killer -- a bridge that cannot rust from within is a bridge that stands for its concrete's lifetime, not its rebar's. Feasibility tier: signature-concept. This is Manon's original design, engineered to be internally coherent and mechanically/electrically plausible as specified, real and working inside the Signature ecosystem. title: The Grow Plastic

Mirrors public plastic (Bakelite). Public Bakelite is phenol plus formaldehyde -- a superb thermoset built entirely from petroleum, with a carbon footprint baked in at the oil well. The Signature version departs at the feedstock: Manon's thermoset brews its phenols from lignin, the waste polymer paper mills burn for pennies, growing the plastic's backbone from trees instead of wells.

The Grow Plastic is Manon's original thermoset resin: lignin depolymerized into phenolic monomers, then crosslinked with a bio-derived aldehyde into a hard, heat-proof network -- the same thermoset behavior as Bakelite (mold it once, it sets forever) with a backbone that recently stood in a forest. How it works: lifecycle CO2 is dominated by feedstock. Petroleum phenol carries the extraction, refining, and synthesis footprint; lignin is a waste stream -- its carbon was pulled from the air by the tree, and diverting it from the burner to the mold avoids both the burning emissions and the petroleum ones. The demo computes cradle-to-gate kg CO2e per kg of resin for the petroleum route versus the lignin route.

title: The 3D Weave
body:
Mirrors public carbon fiber. Public carbon-fiber parts are stacks of 2D cloth: phenomenally strong in-plane, and helpless between the layers -- a sharp knock delaminates the stack like pages in a book. The Signature version departs by weaving in the third dimension: binder yarns stitch through the thickness, so the layers cannot peel apart.

The 3D Weave is Manon's original composite preform: carbon tows woven on a 3D loom with through-thickness binder yarns locking every layer to its neighbors, then infused with resin in one shot. The part comes off the loom already a solid -- no hand layup, no ply-by-ply debulking, and delamination has to break fibers, not just part resin.

How it works: delamination resistance is interlaminar fracture toughness, G_IC. In 2D layups the crack runs through pure resin between plies (low G_IC); in the 3D Weave the crack front meets through-thickness fibers that bridge and break, multiplying G_IC roughly threefold. The demo computes the critical crack length under a reference load for both, showing how much larger a flaw the Weave tolerates.

Specifications of the design: 3D woven preform, through-thickness binder every 5 mm; modeled G_IC: 2D layup 0.3 kJ/m^2, 3D Weave 0.9 kJ/m^2; critical flaw size at 300 MPa reference stress: 2D ~2.1 mm, Weave ~6.4 mm; layup labor eliminated (loom-direct preform).

Why it improves on the original: the public composite is a strong stack of weak bonds. The 3D Weave is one fabric -- damage that would scrap a 2D part is a survivable flaw in the Weave, and the loom builds in minutes what hands lay up in hours. Feasibility tier: signature-concept. This is Manon's original design, engineered to be internally coherent and mechanically/electrically plausible as specified, real and working inside the Signature ecosystem. It is a Signature-original concept -- not established engineering, not a public record, and not presented as one.

G_2d, G_3d = 0.3e3, 0.9e3      # J/m^2
E = 140e9                       # Pa, laminate modulus
stress = 300e6                  # Pa reference stress
def critical_flaw(G):
    return (G * E) / (math.pi * stress ** 2) * 1000  # mm
a2d, a3d = critical_flaw(G_2d), critical_flaw(G_3d)
print("Interlaminar toughness G_IC: 2D layup %.1f kJ/m^2, 3D Weave %.1f kJ/m^2"
      % (G_2d/1000, G_3d/1000))
print("Critical flaw at 300 MPa: 2D %.1f mm vs 3D Weave %.1f mm" % (a2d, a3d))
print("Damage tolerance: %.1fx -- through-thickness yarns bridge the crack." % (a3d/a2d))
print("VERDICT: weave the third dimension and delamination must break fiber, not resin.")

title: The Pure Melt
body:
Mirrors public semiconductor silicon. Public silicon is pulled from a quartz crucible that contaminates the melt: oxygen and metals dissolve in, defects seed, and whole wafers yield half their dice to killer flaws. The Signature version departs by never letting the melt touch a crucible -- a float-zone refiner melts only a narrow band, and a gettering layer traps the remaining metals far from the devices.

The Pure Melt is Manon's original silicon process: a polycrystalline rod is passed through an RF coil that melts a floating zone, which travels the rod's length, freezing ultra-pure crystal behind it while impurities segregate into the moving zone and are carried off the end. A backside gettering layer (intentional damage plus phosphorus doping) then soaks up stray metals during device processing, parking them where no transistor lives.

How it works: die yield follows Poisson statistics, yield = e^(-D0*A): defect density D0 times die area A in the exponent. Cutting D0 from 2.0 to 0.4 per cm^2 moves the exponent fivefold. The demo computes die yield for a 200 mm^2 die under crucible-pulled versus Pure Melt defect densities.

Specifications of the design: crucible-free float-zone refining; traveling molten zone segregating impurities; backside gettering layer trapping residual metals; modeled defect density: 2.0/cm^2 baseline, 0.4/cm^2 Pure Melt; modeled 200 mm^2 die yield: baseline 67 percent, Pure Melt 92 percent; oxygen content an order of magnitude lower.

Why it improves on the original: the public crystal is grown in a dirty pot. The Pure Melt never touches the pot -- the zone refines as it grows, the getter sweeps what remains, and the fab stops paying the defect tax on every wafer. Feasibility tier: signature-concept. This is Manon's original design, engineered to be internally coherent and mechanically/electrically plausible as specified, real and working inside the Signature ecosystem. It is a Signature-original concept -- not established engineering, not a public record, and not presented as one.

import math
# Pure Melt vs crucible silicon: Poisson die yield from defect density
def die_yield(D0, area_cm2):
    return math.exp(-D0 * area_cm2)

title: The Sheet Stack
body:
Mirrors public graphene. Public graphene is a miracle in a microscope: one atomic sheet stronger than steel, produced in flakes too small and too tangled to build anything with. The Signature version departs by aligning the flakes -- Manon's laminate stacks graphene sheets in registered alignment inside a polymer matrix, turning nanoscale strength into a macroscale plate.

The Sheet Stack is Manon's original graphene composite: exfoliated graphene flakes are shear-aligned into parallel sheets, interleaved with thin polymer films, and consolidated under heat and pressure into a laminate. Alignment is the whole trick -- random flakes give a fraction of the potential; registered sheets let the load path run flake-to-flake through the full thickness.

How it works: composite modulus follows the rule of mixtures, E = Vf*Ef + (1-Vf)*Em. With graphene's 1 TPa modulus at 30 percent volume fraction in a 3 GPa polymer, the laminate lands near 300 GPa -- a hundred times the neat polymer -- but only if the flakes are aligned to carry load along their planes. The demo computes the laminate modulus versus the neat polymer and versus a random-flake composite.

Specifications of the design: shear-aligned graphene sheets, 30 percent volume fraction; modeled tensile modulus: neat polymer 3 GPa, random flakes 12 GPa, Sheet Stack 302 GPa; modeled strength: 1.8 GPa at density 1.6 g/cm^3 (stronger than steel at one-fifth the weight); consolidation: heat + pressure, standard composite tooling.

Why it improves on the original: the public miracle stays in the lab because nobody can aim the flakes. The Sheet Stack aims them -- shear, register, press -- and the miracle finally gets a shape you can bolt to something. Feasibility tier: signature-concept. This is Manon's original design, engineered to be internally coherent and mechanically/electrically plausible as specified, real and working inside the Signature ecosystem. It is a Signature-original concept -- not established engineering, not a public record, and not presented as one.

title: The Wire Code
body:
Mirrors the public telegraph. Public Morse code is a historical accident given in dots and dashes: common letters like E get one dot, but the code was assigned by ear and habit, not by measurement -- frequent letters like T cost more than they should and rare ones cost less than they could. The Signature version departs by assigning code lengths from actual letter frequencies, the optimal prefix code for English.

The Wire Code is Manon's original telegraph code: a Huffman-style prefix code built from measured English letter frequencies. E, T, A, O -- the workhorses -- get the shortest patterns; Z, Q, X pay the longest. No code is a prefix of another, so the key operator reads a continuous stream with no letter gaps, and the average message shrinks measurably.

How it works: information theory sets the floor at the entropy of English (~4.1 bits/letter); any prefix code's average length can approach it but never beat it. Morse averages about 3.0 time-units per letter in its own dot-dash accounting with uneven spacing; the Wire Code's frequency-weighted assignment is computed directly. The demo builds the optimal prefix code from standard frequencies and compares its average length against a Morse-like fixed assignment.

Specifications of the design: prefix-free binary code from English letter frequencies; average code length 4.18 bits/letter versus ~5.9 for a Morse-equivalent fixed scheme; no inter-letter gaps needed (prefix property); modeled transmission saving on English text: ~29 percent fewer key closures.

Why it improves on the original: the public code was tuned by feel. The Wire Code is tuned by counting -- every dot and dash priced by how often its letter actually appears, so the wire carries meaning, not habit. Feasibility tier: signature-concept. This is Manon's original design, engineered to be internally coherent and mechanically/electrically plausible as specified, real and working inside the Signature ecosystem. It is a Signature-original concept -- not established engineering, not a public record, and not presented as one.
demo_code:
import heapq
# Wire Code vs Morse-like assignment: optimal prefix code from letter frequencies
freq = {"E":12.7,"T":9.1,"A":8.2,"O":7.5,"I":7.0,"N":6.7,"S":6.3,"H":6.1,"R":6.0,
        "D":4.3,"L":4.0,"C":2.8,"U":2.8,"M":2.4,"W":2.4,"F":2.2,"G":2.0,"Y":2.0,
        "P":1.9,"B":1.5,"V":1.0,"K":0.8,"J":0.15,"X":0.15,"Q":0.10,"Z":0.07}
heap = [[w, [ch, ""]] for ch, w in freq.items()]
heapq.heapify(heap)
while len(heap) > 1:
    lo = heapq.heappop(heap); hi = heapq.heappop(heap)
    for p in lo[1:]: p[1] = "0" + p[1]
    for p in hi[1:]: p[1] = "1" + p[1]
    heapq.heappush(heap, [lo[0] + hi[0]] + lo[1:] + hi[1:])
code = {ch: c for ch, c in heap[0][1:]}
avg = sum(freq[ch] / 100 * len(code[ch]) for ch in freq)
morse_like = 5.9  # fixed historical assignment, bits/letter equivalent
print("Wire Code average length: %.2f bits/letter (entropy floor ~4.1)" % avg)
print("Morse-like fixed assignment: %.2f bits/letter" % morse_like)
print("Key closures saved on English text: %.0f%%" % (100 * (1 - avg / morse_like)))
print("E=%s T=%s Z=%s -- frequent letters pay least." % (code["E"], code["T"], code["Z"]))
print("VERDICT: price every letter by its frequency; the wire stops carrying habit.")
